rows.en: We have already said that yet another kind of correction in Holy Scripture was attributed to the Scribes. This is that they sometimes corrected some expression which, in their opinion, was not fitting to be said in this way with regard to God; therefore they corrected it by choosing another expression, in order to give honor to God; and they point to eighteen places which the Scribes corrected in this manner. But we also said that in most of these places there is no compelling reason to say that they are corrections; yet the root of this view is without doubt strong and received, and not only have we no reason to deny it, but we must admit its truth, since we see from some places in Holy Scripture that the hand of correctors ruled over them, and we have found no time more fit for such work than the time of the Scribes. Now for the purpose we have stated they sometimes exchanged one word for another,{v1_04_15:2} or changed the form of the word or the position of the parts of the sentence, whereby a different sense is given to the sentence;{v1_04_15:3} and so too they sometimes omitted whole passages for some reason and purpose.{v1_04_15:4} And now we shall see that a number of things in Holy Scripture as well, which appear from their content to be appendices and are marked by signs and indications showing that they are later than the time of the composition of the book in which they are found, are also to be counted among the corrections which the Scribes made. And they did a great thing in this, in that they preserved for us various precious writings which prophets and sages of the early generations composed, and which were scattered scroll by scroll; and they gathered them and attached them in the proper place, to teach us, to help us understand the words of the book to which they were attached, for a fuller understanding; and for this reason the name by which they were called befits them: ba'alei asufot [masters of collections]. Indeed, even though we have no clear reports on all these things that reach back to the time of the Scribes, but have relied on late reports, nevertheless it appears that this was really so, since the existence of all the corrections mentioned cannot be denied, and anyone who has eyes will see that they are really found in fact; and we have no reason to attribute them to others than the Scribes alone, for they were the men whose office was to refine and purify our Holy Scriptures, and to them the authority was given.
The sayings of the Scribes and their ordinances.

From the day when religion renewed its youth like the eagle [Psalms 103:5] through the Scribes, with Ezra at their head, they began to build a fence and enacted ordinances for the benefit of the nation and the religion. But in the course of time the ordinances and decrees were fruitful and multiplied in every generation without end. And since they did not become the work of [one] man until most of the sages of the generation agreed upon them, who were counted and concluded to establish and found them, no particular founder's name was called upon them, for the founders were many; rather they were always called by the name divrei soferim [words of the Scribes]. But we must be very, very cautious in understanding this expression, for sometimes the sages of the Talmud used it loosely and said divrei soferim without meaning the early Scribes.{v1_04_16:1} But there are various things which were said in the name of the Scribes and are clearly from them. Of sayings stated specifically in the name of the sages of this generation, only one has reached us. It is the line and measure which the Men of the Great Assembly gave for how the Scribes should conduct themselves in their office, saying: "Be deliberate in judgment, raise up many disciples, and make a fence for the Torah" (Avot 1:2⚠1). The sages of the Mishnah and the Talmud attributed many ordinances to them. The order of the Eighteen prayers, which are called by the general name Tefillah (Megillah 17b), is in their opinion an ordinance of the Men of the Great Assembly. And this tradition is true in some respect. For how can we imagine to ourselves the founding of the worship of God in the Temple unless we say that they made ordinances concerning prayer? But we cannot say with certainty that the very wording of the Eighteen-benediction prayer is the very one that was handed down to us from the Men of the Great Assembly as we have it today.{v1_04_16:2} But the root of the Talmud's tradition, that the Men of the Great Assembly enacted prayers, is true. The one part of the prayers and thanksgivings consisted of various psalms which they selected from the psalms in the book of Psalms. Already in very early times it was the custom to sing songs of praise and thanksgiving to God, but without doubt they selected for themselves psalms suited to that time, and made corrections in them, additions or omissions, as they needed (above, chs. 3 and 6). They also composed new praises and songs, to sing them in the choirs in the Temple. The Hallel which it is our custom to recite on the festivals is one of the children of that time. Yet not all of it; rather it is composed of two parts. The one part begins with Halleluyah and ends with Halleluyah, and the second part begins with Hodu and ends with Hodu. The first part was not composed before the exile, and perhaps after it. So it appears from the images in which it depicts the idols (Psalms 115:4–7), which are close to the images of the prophet in the appendices to Isaiah; and from the rebukes against the idolatrous nations, since this practice too is not found in any of the prophets who preceded that prophet (De Wette in his commentary on Psalms); and it speaks of the troubles that befell them in the past and of the deliverance in the present (115). And this Hallel the Men of the Great Assembly ordained to be recited on the festivals (*Moreh Nevukhei ha-Zeman*, gate 11). The second part was added later, in the days of the Maccabees, as appears from the content of the whole psalm (118) from beginning to end; and there is not in all of it even one saying that does not suit the time of the Maccabees. Therefore we have seen, at any rate, that the first part was composed in the time we are dealing with, or a little before it, and its recitation was ordained by the Men of the Great Assembly or the Scribes.{v1_04_17:1} The second part of the prayers, of which we can say with certainty that it is the work of the Scribes, is: the first three and the last three benedictions of the Eighteen. The custom, still practiced today, of saying the first and last benedictions on Sabbaths and festivals as well is also a sign that they are very ancient, and the ancient custom has remained in our hands (Zunz, p. 36). So too it appears from the prayer Havinenu: although the sages permitted this short prayer to be said at times when the hour requires it, nevertheless they gave no permission to shorten the first and last benedictions, and permitted doing so only with the middle ones (Berakhot 28b⚠2 and Yerushalmi Ta'anit 2:2). This is because from of old these benedictions were more precious in value than the middle ones.{v1_04_17:2} Besides these prayers, further prayers and blessings, and kiddushot and havdalot, were attributed to the Men of the Great Assembly, in order (Berakhot 33). They also attributed to them the reading of the Megillah and its conditions (Megillah 2a), and the writing of the books of Ezekiel, the Twelve, Daniel and the Scroll of Esther (Bava Batra 4a⚠3). To Ezra in particular they attributed ten ordinances (Bava Kamma 82a), and so too the ordinance that the curses in Leviticus be read before Shavuot and the curses in Deuteronomy before Rosh Hashanah (Megillah 31a⚠4). But who knows whether the sages of the Talmud who attributed all these to them relied on a clear tradition? And who can deny that they sometimes attributed things and ordinances to them, or to other ancients, not because the matter was clear to them, but because the beginning of their origin was already hidden from them, and so they hung them on ancient enactors? If we consider the ten ordinances which they attributed to Ezra, we find that among them there are ordinances whose foundation lies in a late time.{v1_04_18:1} And the limit for attributing things to the ancients was not the time of Ezra; that is to say, the later sages attributed new things, lately come, not only to Ezra and the sages of his time, but went many more steps back along the path of time. How many ordinances and customs they attributed to the prophets! They said that the water libation and the encircling of the altar with the willow on the festival of Sukkot is a foundation of the prophets or a custom of the prophets (Yerushalmi Sukkah 4:1, and the Bavli there, 44a). It is very far-fetched to conclude that those who said so relied on a tradition handed down from generation to generation without anyone disputing it, for we find a difference in their opinions: these said so, and another says the water libation is a word of the Torah and derived it from a slight hint in the verse, and there is one who says that they had it by tradition back to Moses at Sinai. Of necessity all these sages spoke only by conjecture and not by relying on a clear tradition; and the truth is that the source of the custom was already hidden from them, and each one pointed to its source according to his opinion.{v1_04_18:2} So too they attributed to the prophets the two festival days of Rosh Hashanah (Eruvin 3:9 in the Yerushalmi). This too appears not to have been said by the sages from tradition, and in the Babylonian Talmud there is no mention of it; surely this is nothing but the conjecture of individual sages, who thought so because, since from of old they sanctified the month by sighting, it is self-evident that they were mostly compelled to make Rosh Hashanah two days, and from the time when the sanctification of the month by sighting began they made Rosh Hashanah two days. But since they did not know to what time this correction should be ascribed, they hung it on the early prophets.{v1_04_18:3} And without doubt in this conjecture they relied on their midrash which they expounded on the words of Ezekiel, who says of the prophets who see vanity that "they shall not be in the council of My people" (Ezekiel 13), where in their view this council [sod] is the secret [sod] of intercalation, and the prophets who see vanity shall not be in the secret of intercalation (Ketubbot 112b; Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 1:2). From this we see that they understood Ezekiel's words as ascribing the secret of intercalation to the faithful prophets, and this was the root of their conjecture when they attributed the ordinance of the two days of Rosh Hashanah to the prophets as well. To Haggai the prophet too they attributed three testimonies. From their content it appears that those who said so had no clarified tradition about it, but relied on an aggadah which the Talmud cast doubt upon, not believing that it ever came out of the mouth of Haggai the prophet (Yevamot 16a, and Tosafot s.v. Rabbi; and see the Yerushalmi there). Likewise they attributed the part of the Grace after Meals that speaks of the remembrance of Jerusalem to King David, and attributed to his son Solomon the ordinance that one say in the Grace after Meals "for the great and holy House" (Berakhot 48b); and certainly they said this only by way of conjecture. This is because David truly established that Jerusalem should be the royal city and supreme over all the cities, and because Solomon built the Temple; therefore they moved the time of the ordinance back to the earliest time to which it was possible to advance it, and they did not place it later, because they did not know on whom else to hang it. But the truth is that all the benedictions of the Grace after Meals as we have them originate from a very late time, and there is not even one saying in them in which the signs of youth are not recognizable. (And see Naḥmanides in his glosses on the *Sefer ha-Mitzvot* and the novellae of R. Solomon ibn Adret.) And everything besides these that they attributed to the earliest of the early generations and to their heads, its character testifies of it that it is the product of a late time. But they searched and sought hints in the words of those ancients only so as to have some small support to lean on in attributing to them the ordinance which, for some reason (sometimes known and sometimes not known to us), they wished to give a place in ancient years. So it appears clearly in all that they attributed to David and Solomon (Eruvin 21b; Yevamot 21a) and in what they attributed to Jehoshaphat king of Judah (Pesaḥim 92a): it all rests on slight hints according to the ways of aggadic midrash. And so too it is with many ordinances that were attributed to Ezra or to other sages in these early generations: they did not attribute them to them because they had clear knowledge that it was so, but since the time of their birth was hidden from them, they searched and sought to find some hint in the words of the heads of the ancient generations so that they might hang on them the founding of some ordinance; and even if they had no hint they would hang it on them, because the generation of Ezra was the first in which they began to enact ordinances and build fences.{v1_04_19:1}

footnotes.en: Wherever ra'ah is found in the Nif'al, it is only with the relational preposition, in combination with el, al or le-. Therefore, wherever the root ra'ah is used with et ha-Shem or et Elohim, the text had the Qal, and they corrected the reading to the Nif'al out of reverence. And we found "When shall I come and appear before God [penei Elohim]" (Psalms 42), and the Nif'al here too is a correction of the Scribes. And we find "appears unto God [el Elohim]" (ibid. 84), and it appears from this that this psalm is late, since the author himself was already careful and wrote yera'eh in the Nif'al and in combination with the relational preposition.

The commentators on Scripture inquired into the root of the qeri and ketiv. R. David Kimḥi and Don Isaac Abravanel wrote in agreement with what we have written, and the author of the introduction to the *Mikra'ot Gedolot*, Venice printing, cried out like a crane against them; but in all his words we see no proof and no just judgment, only noise. And see also the *Efodi*, ch. 6⚠1, Vienna printing.

1.note: Second letter faint; read ו, could be ז.

footnotes.en: The intention is to some of the places which according to the Mekhilta, the Tanḥuma and Midrash Rabbah are corrections of the Scribes. For in some of them the law is with them. One of them is 2 Samuel⚠1 3:13, "for the iniquity which he knew, because his sons cursed themselves [lahem]." On this the authors of the midrash said that it is a correction of the Scribes; and in the opinion of the commentators lo [him] was written in place of lahem; but this is not the intention of the midrash; rather Elohim was written, and they omitted the alef and yod out of reverence. And perhaps in other places, where Scripture tells of a curse with which one of the persons cursed God, Scripture turns its language from a curse to a blessing, as "Naboth blessed God" (1 Kings 21:13), "bless God and die" (Job 1:9⚠2), and others besides; perhaps these too are corrections of the Scribes. "And curse by his king and by his god" (Isaiah 8:21) they did not correct, because it refers to the idols, not to the God of Israel, as in the Targum Jonathan and all the Jewish commentators; and the commentators who take it the other way are mistaken.

1.note: The verse is 1 Samuel 3:13; kept as printed.

2.note: The verse is Job 2:9; kept as printed.

footnotes.en: I mean the verse "and Abraham stood yet before the Lord" (Genesis 18:22), where too the words of the midrash are right that this is a correction of the Scribes, the Men of the Great Assembly. For according to the sequence of the passage it is clearly proved that it should be "and the Lord stood yet before Abraham," but they corrected it out of reverence toward on High.

I already hinted above, in ch. 3, in a note, that in a number of the psalms they made additions for the needs of their time, when they used them in the Temple. And it seems that they also corrected and took away. The psalm Tehillah le-David [Psalm 145] was in my opinion one of the psalms they used in their prayer in very early times, and therefore the sages of the Talmud gave it great value for every early prayer⚠1. The psalm is built on the alphabet, and the letter nun is missing from it, and in the Talmud they gave the reason that it contains the downfall of Israel. But this reason is only an aggadic homily; the main point is that the verse with the letter nun was not suited to their purpose, namely for prayer, so they omitted it. And in the psalm "I will bless the Lord at all times" [Psalm 34] it appears clearly that the connection is very difficult between the verse "The face of the Lord is against them that do evil" etc. and the verse after it, "They cried, and the Lord heard" etc.: to whom does it refer in saying "they cried"? And who are those who cry? But it appears that the last verse, "The Lord redeems the soul of His servants" etc., was the letter pe in the psalm, and was written in place of "The face of the Lord is against them that do evil," so that "they cried, and the Lord heard" refers, that is, to His servants who trust in Him. But so as not to end with an evil thing, "Evil shall slay the wicked" etc., they ended with the verse "The Lord redeems," and added the verse "The face of the Lord," although it has no proper connection with what follows. And I heard that R. Solomon Judah Rapoport also remarked on this. Other examples like these are found, and it is not marvelous nor far-fetched if I say that this was the work of the Scribes, since they were the enactors of the earliest prayers, and they also made other corrections in Holy Scripture. R. Abraham Geiger has already dealt at length with this point in his book *Urschrift*, but he exceeded the measure; whoever wishes to understand the matter and enter into its depth should look there, and for us, for the sake of the work before us, what we have written is enough.

1.note: Sense unclear: perhaps 'great value, above every early prayer'.

footnotes.en: In the Yerushalmi, Berakhot 1:7, it speaks of words of the School of Hillel and calls them divrei soferim. And so in the Bavli, Rosh Hashanah (19a), it calls the days of Megillat Ta'anit divrei soferim, and so it is in Ta'anit (17b). And in Tractate Yadayim 3:2 they said that [the rule] that Holy Scriptures render the hands impure is from the words of the Scribes, and in truth it is one of the eighteen matters; see there in the commentators on the Mishnah. And in Niddah (69b) they said of the impurity of the flux of idolaters that it is from the words of the Scribes, and the essence of this decree is only from Hillel. For this decree is one with the decree mentioned in Shabbat (83a), that they decreed that they be like zavim in all respects, so that an Israelite child should not become familiar with them in sodomy (see Niddah 34a and Rashi's commentary); and if so, it is the very decree that they decreed on an idolatrous child, that he be impure through flux for this reason, and in the opinion of the Talmud (Shabbat 17b) it is one of the eighteen matters. And in the Sifra, parashat Shemini, ch. 8, it is stated: R. Yose says, there is no impurity of liquids by Torah law, only by the words of the Scribes. And so Rabbi proved, according to the words of R. Yose; and R. Eliezer⚠1 says there is no impurity of liquids at all, and his proof is from Yose ben Yo'ezer, who testified concerning the liquids of the slaughterhouse that they are clean. Now R. Yose, who said there is impurity of liquids by the words of the Scribes, necessarily did not mean the early Scribes, since in the days of Yose ben Yo'ezer the decree did not yet exist. And you will find much more of this kind.

1.note: Abbreviation expanded as R. Eliezer; it could stand for another sage.

footnotes.en: In *Bikkurim* for the year 5624, published by R. Naphtali Keller, there is a special essay by me, "Iyyun Tefillah," in which I spoke of the antiquity of the Eighteen Benedictions. My inquiries there are aimed against the author of *Hegyon Lev*, who assigned most of the prayers to the time of the Maccabees and some of them to the time after the destruction; and against this I said that the foundations on which he built are shaky, since we can just as well uphold the tradition of the Talmud that all the prayers are an ordinance of the Men of the Great Assembly, and that some of them were enacted while Israel was still in the Babylonian exile, namely those benedictions whose content shows that they were founded at a time when the Temple was destroyed and Israel was in a bad state. And my intention was to show what the sages of the Talmud saw that led them to say that they are so ancient. But for myself it did not enter my heart, and I did not think, that this was my opinion absolutely. And because in places I was not precise in my language in that essay, I gave the reader occasion to think that I had written my own opinion; and many have already asked me, and many more besides⚠1, for an account of this matter. For this reason I saw fit to remark on it here and to reveal my true intention.

1.note: Phrase from Nahum 1:12 in reversed order; rendered by sense.

footnotes.en: The verses that point to the time of the exile or after it are "Not unto us" etc. up to "He is their help and their shield" (115:1–11) and from "I love" up to "All men are liars" (115⚠1:1–11). Therefore it is possible that these twenty-two verses are a late addition from the time of the exile and after, alluding to the troubles that befell them and to the deliverance by which they were delivered from them. All the rest was composed earlier, and was composed first and foremost for the festival of Passover, and the time of its composition was in the days of Hezekiah, according to the opinion of one of the sages of the Talmud; and it is hinted also in Scripture (2 Chronicles 30:21): "and they praised the Lord day by day." And this is the explanation of the practice of skipping the verses of the addition on the last two⚠2 days of Passover, in memory of the ancient custom. The second part was composed first and foremost as thanksgiving for the deliverance in the days of the Maccabees, and therefore it belongs chiefly to Ḥanukkah; and in this you will find the answer to the question of the Gemara (Arakhin 10b), why Hallel is not said on Purim while it is said on Ḥanukkah.

1.note: Printed as 115; the verses 'I love ... all men are liars' are Psalm 116:1–11.

2.note: As printed; the shortened Hallel is said on the last six days of Passover.

footnotes.en: The benediction Avodah in the version before us is already corrected and is not the old one; see Berakhot (11b) and Yoma (68b), with Rashi's commentary. And the author of *Hegyon Lev* wrote that also the second benediction, namely Gevurot⚠1, did not remain in its original form, but several sayings were added to it which repeat again and again the mention of the resurrection of the dead, in order to remove [it] from the heart of the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection of the dead; and this sect of deniers arose only at a late time, in the days of Antigonus of Sokho. Thus far the words of the author of *Hegyon Lev*. But I am not comfortable with this effort to find in every saying of the early sages a special intention to oppose holders of other opinions. It is true that from the words of the sages of every generation, whether written or oral, we can judge the opinions that ruled at the time they were said or composed; and therefore from the second benediction too, "Atah Gibbor," which speaks from beginning to end of the principle of faith in the resurrection of the dead, one may judge that at the time it was composed the heads of the generation strove to establish faith in the resurrection of the dead in the heart of the people. But we see in this no necessity to conclude that they repeated the mention of this belief with great precision because its deniers were already a separate sect. Know for yourself: in the first benediction, "Avot," they also repeated the mention of the merit of the fathers, and this is certainly not aimed against a sect of deniers; rather they wished to strengthen trust in God's deliverance for the sake of the fathers of the world; so too they wished to strengthen trust in the reward of the world to come in the second benediction.

In Bava Kamma (82a) the "immersion of one who has had a seminal emission" is counted among the ordinances of Ezra, and in the Yerushalmi Shabbat ch. 2 they attribute it to the court of Shammai and Hillel. So too the ordinance of havdalot is doubtful; and see *Hegyon Lev*, p. 406.

The custom of bringing palm branches and willow to every rejoicing was an old custom, as is explicit in the Torah, which links the rejoicing to the taking of the four species. And in the days of Simeon the Hasmonean, when they captured the citadel in Jerusalem, they entered it and rejoiced with song and with palm branches (1 Maccabees ch. 3, 53⚠1); and in 2 Maccabees (ch. 10, 7⚠2) willow is mentioned in the rejoicing. And the custom of the water libation seems to have been founded on an aggadah which tells that the priests hid the fire of the altar, and when they came up from the exile Nehemiah found the place, but they found no fire in it, only water; and they took of the water and poured it on the altar, and a miracle happened, that the fire of God came and consumed the sacrifice. And that day they made a festival in memory of the miracle. So it is told in Maccabees (2 Maccabees 1:22–41⚠3). We do not wish to inquire into the nature of the miracle. But this emerges for us from it: that at that time they celebrated a festival on which, according to the story of the miracle, Nehemiah found the fire and poured water on the altar; and therefore this is the foundation of the custom of the water libation.
